beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear, with a short film for INFO seventy-three seventy-five, Computational Skepticism for AI. You might think better instruments will eventually show us everything. They won't. Every instrument hands you a sharper slice of the world. The real question is whether you know it's a slice.

beats.narration_text: Four terms. Phenomena: the world as it appears to a mind. Noomenna: things as they are in themselves. Category: a concept the mind supplies to every experience, like cause and effect. And the slice: the part of the world you can actually observe.

the part of the world you can observe

beats.narration_text: The idea comes from Immanuel Kahnt, in the Critique of Pure Reason, from seventeen eighty-one, with a second edition in seventeen eighty-seven. Kahnt split the world in two. Phenomena: things as they appear to a mind. Noomenna: things as they are in themselves. Everything you have ever seen is on the near side of that line.

beats.narration_text: We know appearances. The thing in itself we can think, but never know. In Kahnt's words: while we surrender the power of cognizing, we still reserve the power of thinking objects, as things in themselves. And he never said the thing isn't there. An appearance without something that appears, he wrote, would be absurd.

shot.visual_intent: Same cast. A solid sight line from the lens stops at the frame with an ink cross ('know'); a dashed thought line arcs over the frame to the dark block and lands with a check ('think'); the dark block pulses: it is there.

the thing pulses: it is there

beats.narration_text: Where does the frame come from? Not from the world. From us. Space and time, Kahnt said, are the forms of our sensibility: the shape every experience must take before we can have it. And cause and effect is one of the categories: a concept the understanding brings to experience, not a feature it reads off the world. Everything you will ever see arrives already framed.

shot.visual_intent: The frame slides back from mid-stage and docks onto the front of the mind box; three labels land beside it one by one ('space', 'time', 'cause'); the appearance re-forms through the docked frame.

show.event: the frame lifts off the world

shot.motion_claim: The frame slides back from mid-stage and docks onto the front of the mind box; three labels land beside it one by one ('space', 'time', 'cause'); the appearance re-forms through the docked frame.

beats.narration_text: Take gravity. You never see it. You see the apple fall. You see the orbit bend. The cause, you infer. David Hume had made that a problem: we never perceive the connection, only one thing following another. Kahnt wrote of him: the suggestion of David Hume was the very thing, which many years ago first interrupted my dogmatic slumber. His answer, in the Proleg-omena of seventeen eighty-three: the connection comes from us. Cause is a rule the mind applies to what it sees. That is why Bear calls gravity almost a textbook Kantian example.

shot.visual_intent: The mind with its docked frame ('cause'); an apple drops from a kraft ledge and lands ('seen'); a dot rides an ink ellipse around a kraft sphere ('seen'); a dashed ink link joins the two with a label ('inferred'); the 'cause' label pulses.

beats.narration_text: So will better instruments close the gap? Kahnt says no. And not because instruments are weak. Any possible experience still comes through space, time and the categories. In his words: carry our empirical intuition even to the very highest degree of clearness, and we should not thereby advance one step nearer to a knowledge of the constitution of objects as things in themselves. A better telescope gives you a sharper slice. Not a bigger one.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft telescope on a stand between the mind and the dark thing; a pale wedge of view from its lens to the thing; a bigger lens swaps in and the wedge's edges turn from ghost to ink while its angle stays ('sharper'); the appearance gains detail lines; the thing beyond the wedge stays dark ('not bigger').

show.event: a bigger lens: the wedge sharpens

shot.motion_claim: A kraft telescope on a stand between the mind and the dark thing; a pale wedge of view from its lens to the thing; a bigger lens swaps in and the wedge's edges turn from ghost to ink while its angle stays ('sharper'); the appearance gains detail lines; the thing beyond the wedge stays dark ('not bigger').

beats.narration_text: Bear doesn't go that far. This is Bear's view, not Kahnt's. The gap is permanent, but contingent: finite minds, ever-better tools, approaching without arriving. Asymptotic. Kahnt's gap is shut in principle, by the very form of experience. Bear's is shut in practice, by how far finite minds and their tools can reach. This film holds both. Know which one you're holding.

shot.visual_intent: Two panels. Left: a small mind and a dark thing with an ink wall between them ('in principle'). Right ('Bear's view'): an ink curve climbs toward a dashed limit line and never touches it; small kraft tool boxes step up along it; a terracotta end dot ('asymptotic').

beats.narration_text: So here is the humility. We only ever see a slice. And there are two kinds of not-seeing. The first is what lies outside the slice. The second is harder: forgetting that there is an outside at all. Picture a lantern in a large dark room. The lit patch is your slice. The walls you can't see are still there. Keep both in mind: what's outside the patch, and that there is an outside.

show.event: the lantern and its lit patch: the slice
the walls you can't see: outside

beats.narration_text: One line about AI. A model's confidence is confidence about its slice: the data it was trained on, the inputs it was given. It says nothing about what lies outside the patch. When a model sounds sure, ask what its lantern was lighting.

shot.visual_intent: The same room; a dark model block sits in the lit patch with kraft pages inside the light ('model'); a check lands on the pages ('its slice'); ghost outlines of unlit objects sit on the floor beyond the patch.

show.event: the model in the lit patch
a check on its data: its slice

shot.motion_claim: The same room; a dark model block sits in the lit patch with kraft pages inside the light ('model'); a check lands on the pages ('its slice'); ghost outlines of unlit objects sit on the floor beyond the patch.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one thing you, or a model you use, are confident about, and paste this into Claude: Here is one thing I, or a model I use, am confident about: describe it. Split it into three lists: what I can actually observe, what I am inferring from those observations, and one thing that lies outside my slice, which I have no way to observe at all. For each observed item, say how it was observed. Then check two things yourself. Is every item you called observed really observed? And did you name something genuinely unobservable, not merely unchecked?
